nameStory: This bright yellow, greasy fungus gets its spooky name from its slippery, butter-like texture and mysterious appearance on dead branches during dark, rainy weather. Folk tales once attributed such strange forest growths to witches' midnight activities, and the name stuck because of how the fungus feels exactly like someone smeared golden butter on a tree branch.
description: Witch's butter is a bright orange-yellow jelly fungus that looks like someone splattered colorful Jell-O on dead tree branches. Its surface is deeply wrinkled and folded, resembling a squishy brain or crumpled tissue paper. The fungus can grow up to 3 inches across and has a distinctly gelatinous, slippery texture that's greasy to the touch when wet. After dry weather, it shrivels into a thin, almost unrecognizable film but magically plumps back up after rain.

idTips.label: Gelatinous texture
idTips.description: Touch it gently - it feels exactly like firm Jell-O or wet rubber, with a distinctly greasy, slippery surface that's unlike any other forest growth

idTips.label: Bright yellow-orange color
idTips.description: Vibrant golden-yellow to orange coloration that's hard to miss against dark bark, like a splash of bright paint on the forest floor

idTips.label: Wrinkled, brain-like surface
idTips.description: Deeply folded and convoluted surface with lobes and creases that look remarkably like a miniature brain or crumpled wet paper

idTips.label: Location on dead branches
idTips.description: Always found on dead but still-attached branches or recently fallen wood, never on living trees or the ground itself

idTips.label: Weather-responsive growth
idTips.description: Plump and prominent during or after rain, then shrinks to a barely visible thin film during dry spells

idTips.label: Size and clustering
idTips.description: Individual masses range from marble-sized to 3 inches across, often appearing in multiple clusters along the same dead branch

habitat: Look for witch's butter in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially on dead branches of hardwood trees like oak, maple, and birch. It thrives in moist woodland areas where fallen branches accumulate, from lowland forests to mid-elevation slopes. You'll often find it in the same areas where other wood-decay fungi are actively breaking down dead wood.

seasonality.spring: Most visible during wet spring weather when frequent rains keep the fungus plump and gelatinous. Look for bright yellow masses appearing seemingly overnight on dead branches after rain showers.
seasonality.summer: Present but may shrivel during dry spells, becoming almost invisible as thin films. After summer thunderstorms, watch for rapid rehydration and the return of the characteristic jelly-like appearance.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for spotting witch's butter as autumn rains and humidity provide ideal conditions. The bright yellow stands out beautifully against colorful fall foliage and darkening bark.
seasonality.winter: Remains present but often shriveled and inconspicuous during freezing weather. During winter thaws and rain, it can still plump up and become visible on snow-free branches.

funFact: Witch's butter is actually a vampire fungus that parasitizes other fungi - it doesn't break down wood directly but instead attacks and feeds on wood-decay fungi that are already doing the hard work of decomposing dead branches.
confusionNotes: Other jelly fungi can look similar, but witch's butter's bright golden-yellow color and exclusive growth on dead wood makes it distinctive. Orange jelly fungi tend to be more reddish, while other gelatinous fungi are usually brown, white, or translucent - remember 'butter yellow' for this species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its magical name, witch's butter is actually considered edible and is cultivated in some parts of the world for food and medicine. However, its bland taste and slimy texture make it more of a survival food than a culinary delight in North American cuisine.
compareHints: Unlike its relative snow fungus which is white and primarily found in warmer climates, witch's butter is distinctly yellow-orange and thrives in New England's temperate forests. The other Tremella species in our region are much less common and tend to be smaller, growing as tiny parasites on lichens rather than forming the large, conspicuous masses that make witch's butter so noticeable.
